\subsection{Unit 7: Points to ponder}
\label{\detokenize{AssignmentThree/main:unit-7-points-to-ponder}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Hector Barquero posted Mar 21, 2026 8:35 PM
\sphinxurl{https://learning.athabascau.ca/d2l/le/18658/discussions/threads/350740/View}

\sphinxAtStartPar
I compared differences to javascript and the main differences I found were mutability. I forgot that there was a subtle difference, you can’t mutate strings in js, but you can in cpp.

\sphinxAtStartPar
I also forgot that s.find is a member function in cpp and returns string::npos when there’s nothing found, but in javascript it returns \sphinxhyphen{}1 (indexOf) and is a method you use on the string itself.


\subsection{Unit 8: Points to ponder}
\label{\detokenize{AssignmentThree/main:unit-8-points-to-ponder}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Hector Barquero posted Jun 8, 2026 3:42 PM
\sphinxurl{https://learning.athabascau.ca/d2l/le/18658/discussions/threads/391920/View}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Reading this chapter took me a long time, since I took a small hiatus from AU coursework\textendash{} but I’m back and was pleasantly surprised that things were ramping up in this chapter since we’ve moved from thinking about “just writing code” to now thinking about the tech debt of our mathematical calculations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Instead of passing regular vars, we’re now looking at structs and compound types, doing things like call by values and call by refs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is fun for me because compared to javascript, c++ makes these concepts explicit. In js, objects are passed around and object shapes change at runtime whereas c++ forces you to think about the structure of your data, if you want to copy it, and how you’ll pass it within functions. It feels like a step away for me from writing code to now writing calculations, and that’s fun.


\subsection{Unit 9: Points to ponder}
\label{\detokenize{AssignmentThree/main:unit-9-points-to-ponder}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Hector Barquero posted Jun 12, 2026 4:05 AM
\sphinxurl{https://learning.athabascau.ca/d2l/le/18658/discussions/threads/394111/View}

\sphinxAtStartPar
I found this chapter a lighter read since it was less about syntax and more about design choices. One neat difference from what I’m used to is that c++ lets you declare const with a reference, for example:

\sphinxAtStartPar
const \&foo n

\sphinxAtStartPar
where you’re essentially saying: “hey use this original object, don’t copy it, and make it immutable”. Javascript doesn’t have that, so it’s neat for me to remember that’s a thing. Objects in js are mutable and passed around with reference\sphinxhyphen{}like behaviour by default, but in c++ you’re constantly thinking about choices between copying, modifying the original or a read only\sphinxhyphen{}like behaviour:

\sphinxAtStartPar
for ex:
foo n \textless{}\textendash{} copy
foo \&n \textless{}\textendash{} modify original
const n \textless{}\textendash{} read only

\sphinxAtStartPar
This chapter was cool because it exposed design patterns and thinking less than syntax, and exposed what other languages like javascript are hiding from you.

\subsection{Unit 7}
\label{\detokenize{AssignmentThree/main:unit-7}}\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 7.1: Containers for strings}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A string stores an ordered sequence of characters in one object.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{std::string}} manages its own storage and can grow or shrink as needed.

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 7.2: string variables}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{string}} variable can be declared, initialized, reassigned, and passed to functions.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
String literals use double quotes.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{std::string}} belongs to the standard library.

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 7.3: Extracting characters from a string}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The subscript operator \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{{[}{]}}} accesses a character by its zero\sphinxhyphen{}based index.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The first character is at index \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{0}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accessing an invalid index produces undefined behaviour.

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 7.4: Length}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{length}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{size}} function returns the number of characters in a string.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The final valid index is one less than the string’s length.

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 7.5: Traversal}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
String traversal visits characters one at a time, usually with a loop.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
An index\sphinxhyphen{}based loop can read or modify each character.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A range\sphinxhyphen{}based loop is useful when the index isn’t needed.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Traversal normally runs in linear time relative to the string length.

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 7.6: A run\sphinxhyphen{}time error}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A run\sphinxhyphen{}time error can occur when a program accesses a string outside its valid range.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The code may compile even though the invalid index only appears during execution.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 7.7: The find function}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{string::find}} returns the first position where a character or substring appears.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
It returns \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{string::npos}} when no match exists.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Searches can optionally begin at a specified index.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 7.8: Our own version of find}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A custom find function scans characters until it locates the target.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
It should return either the matching position or a clear failure value.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Writing the search manually demonstrates traversal, conditions, and early return.

\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 7.9: Looping and counting}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A counter can track how many characters satisfy a condition during traversal.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The counter starts at zero and increases when a match is found.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Counting requires examining every character unless an earlier result is sufficient.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The operation is generally \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{O(n)}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Comparison operators compare strings lexicographically.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar

\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 8.6: Call by value}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar

\begin{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Unit 9}
\label{\detokenize{AssignmentThree/main:unit-9}}\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 9.1: Time}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Time}} structure can group hours, minutes, and seconds.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The representation should define valid ranges for each member.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Related values are easier to pass and return as one object.

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 9.2: printTime}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{printTime}} function formats a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Time}} object for output.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Separating formatting from calculation keeps responsibilities clear.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Padding may be used so minutes and seconds always occupy two digits.

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 9.3: Functions for objects}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Functions can accept objects as parameters and perform type\sphinxhyphen{}specific operations.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Related helper functions form an interface around the object’s representation.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The function name should describe the operation rather than the storage details.

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 9.4: Pure functions}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A pure function returns a result without modifying its arguments or external state.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The same inputs always produce the same output.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pure functions are easier to test and reuse.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
They reduce unexpected interactions between parts of a program.

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 9.5: const parameters}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{const}} reference parameter prevents the function from modifying the supplied object.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
It avoids copying while documenting read\sphinxhyphen{}only intent.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The compiler rejects attempts to change the parameter.

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 9.6: Modifiers}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A modifier changes an existing object rather than returning a separate object.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Modifier functions usually take non\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{const}} references.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Their names should make the mutation clear.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Callers must account for the original object’s changed state.

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 9.7: Fill\sphinxhyphen{}in functions}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A fill\sphinxhyphen{}in function writes a result into an object supplied by reference.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
It can avoid constructing a separate return value.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Output parameters should be obvious from the function interface.

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 9.8: Which is best?}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pure functions are usually easier to reason about because they don’t change their inputs.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Modifiers can be useful when updating an existing object is the intended operation.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Fill\sphinxhyphen{}in functions may help when several results must be returned.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The best design depends on clarity, ownership, cost, and expected use.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Consistency matters more than forcing one style everywhere.

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 9.9: Incremental development versus planning}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Incremental development adds and tests one small behaviour at a time.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Up\sphinxhyphen{}front planning defines the representation and major operations before implementation.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Complex tasks often benefit from combining both approaches.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Tests should be added as each step becomes functional.

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 9.10: Generalization}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Generalization replaces fixed assumptions with parameters or reusable operations.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A generalized function can handle more cases without duplicated code.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Abstraction shouldn’t make a simple solution harder to understand.

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{ThinkCScpp 9.11: Algorithms}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
An algorithm is a finite, defined sequence of steps for solving a problem.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Algorithms can be compared by correctness, clarity, time cost, and memory cost.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The same problem may support several valid algorithms.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Input size determines how performance scales.

\end{itemize}
